source_batch.unit_label: Module A unit 7: Risks in Foreign Trade and the role of ECGC

facts.statement: Risks specific to international trade, by who bears them: buyer risk (non-acceptance, non-payment, quality acceptance, credit risk), seller risk (not shipping after advance payment, shipping poor quality or late), shipping risk (intermediaries such as shipping companies, handling agents, port authorities and transporters; goods abandoned, mishandled, wrongly delivered; strikes; container shortage; piracy) and other risks (bank failure, settlement, competition, fraudulent documents, price, legal, spread, market risk). By nature: credit risk (buyer's credit worthiness, non-payment), legal risk (changes in law, embargoes, restrictions on remittance), country and political risk (uncertain laws, weak foreign reserves leading to externalisation issues), operational risk (strikes, system failures, errors) and exchange risk (adverse currency movement, including a stronger home currency or weaker competitor currency).

International trade risks can be mitigated by acting cautiously, planning movement of goods and money, setting counterparty limits, credit insurance (which also covers country risk), forward covers, futures and options, timing inflows and outflows of foreign exchange, and foreign currency accounts; the tools used must be understood and controlled so that they do not add to the original risks.

A bank's Board sets country exposure limits in relation to the bank's regulatory capital (Tier I plus Tier II), reviewed at least once a year; the limit for any country must not exceed regulatory capital, except for the insignificant risk category. Funded exposures (cash and bank balances, deposit placements, investments, loans and advances, trade credits and receivables, vostro overdrafts) and non-funded exposures (letters of credit, committed lines, guarantees, performance and bid bonds, confirmation of foreign banks' letters of credit) from domestic and foreign branches are reckoned. Indirect country risk is taken into account where net funded exposure to a country is one per cent or more of total assets, with indirect exposures reckoned at 50 per cent. Exposures are computed net of collaterals, guarantees and insurance, and netting is allowed for cash collateral, bank guarantees and credit insurance issued in a lower risk category country. The Reserve Bank may prescribe an aggregate limit for the higher risk categories.

The Reserve Bank asks banks to have their own system of grading countries on parameters such as political stability, international relations, economic policy, GDP, inflation, exchange rate volatility, level of foreign trade, balance of payments, external debt, reserves, IMF quotas, international rating, payment track record and overall assessment; banks without their own system may adopt the ECGC classification. ECGC uses a seven-fold classification: A1 insignificant, A2 low, B1 moderately low, B2 moderate, C1 moderately high, C2 high, D very high. Countries in A1 to B2 are open cover; C1 and C2 and D countries are restricted cover. The courseware says a provision is required where exposure to a country is 1 per cent or more of total assets on the balance sheet date.

ECGC Ltd (formerly Export Credit Guarantee Corporation of India) is wholly owned by the Government of India, works under the administrative control of the Ministry of Commerce and Industry and is managed by a Board with representatives of the Government, the Reserve Bank, banking, insurance and the exporting community. The Government set up Export Risks Insurance Corporation in 1957, which became the Export Credit Guarantee Corporation in 1964. Its objectives include encouraging globalisation of India's trade, helping exporters manage credit risk through information on buyers, banks and countries, protecting exporters against buyer, bank or country failure, and helping banks lend by insuring them.

Credit guarantees and policies are issued on a risk-sharing basis: ECGC does not cover 100 per cent of the export value or the finance, and the exporter or the bank shares part of the loss; maximum cover is 90 to 95 per cent. ECGC's schemes are governed by the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority and general insurance rules apply, so premium on financial guarantees is paid in advance (one month's premium up front based on the previous year). Any recovery made by the exporter or bank is shared with ECGC in the ratio of the risk sharing (for example 65:35).

The ECGC Shipment Comprehensive Risks policy is a whole-turnover declaration-based policy for 12 months for an exporter whose anticipated annual turnover is above ₹5 crore, covering commercial or buyer risk, political risk and letter of credit opening bank risk at 90 per cent cover; shipments backed by letters of credit may be excluded; the exporter must hold credit limits on buyers and opening banks, keep premium deposits, declare shipments monthly by the 15th of the next month, declare bills unpaid more than 30 days after due date by the 15th of the next month, claim within 360 days of the due date of the bill or 540 days from policy expiry whichever is earlier, take loss minimisation and recovery steps and share recoveries. It carries a no claim bonus of 5 per cent up to 50 per cent. The courseware describes the standard policies (shipment and contracts, comprehensive and political), cover of 90 per cent, protracted default usually after four months and exclusions: commercial disputes, causes inherent in the goods, failure to obtain import or exchange authorisation, default of an agent or collecting bank, exchange rate fluctuation and the exporter's own failure.
facts.locator: SCR sales literature; S03 printed pp. 191-192, section 7.6 A

facts.statement: Other ECGC policies for exporters, per the courseware: the Small Exporters Policy (a standard policy with improvements for small exporters, with a projected turnover limit and shorter periods), Specific Shipment policies for short-term credit up to 180 days and for deferred payment, buyer's credit, services and construction projects; Exports (Specific Buyers) policy covering all shipments to a named buyer; Buyer Exposure policy covering large exporters on exposure to one buyer; Export Turnover policy for exporters whose premium would be at least ₹10 lakh a year; Consignment Exports policies (stock-holding agent and global entity); IT-Enabled Services policy for a single customer at 80 per cent cover; and the Policy for SME sector (later the Micro Exporters Policy) at 90 per cent cover. Customer specific policies are for large exporters with annual premium above ₹10 lakh.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 190-195, section 7.5.2 and 7.6 B to I, and p. 200

facts.statement: ECGC covers for banks, per the courseware: packing credit insurance (for advances for manufacture, processing, purchase or packing against a firm order or letter of credit, issued for one year; claim payable where the advance is unpaid four months after due date); the whole-turnover covers for packing credit and for post-shipment credit (ECIB WT-PC and WT-PS); the Export Production Finance Guarantee (advances against incentives receivable at pre-shipment stage); the Export Finance Guarantee (post-shipment advances against cash assistance, duty drawback and similar incentives); the Export Performance Indemnity (a counter-guarantee to the bank for guarantees it issues for its exporter clients such as performance and bid bonds); the Export Finance (Overseas Lending) Guarantee (protects a bank that lends foreign currency to an overseas project contractor); and the Transfer Guarantee (protects a bank that confirms a foreign letter of credit against the failure of the foreign bank to reimburse). Premium on WT-PC is borne by exporters and on WT-PS by banks.

Special schemes, per the courseware: the Exchange Fluctuation Risk Cover scheme applies to payments scheduled beyond 12 months up to 15 years in specified currencies, with a deductible of 2 per cent of the reference rate, so gains or losses within 2 per cent are for the exporter and ECGC bears losses beyond 2 per cent up to 35 per cent (and takes gains over 2 per cent up to 35 per cent); maturity factoring provides up to 90 per cent finance, credit protection, a sales ledger and collection, for exporters on open account with a clean record; buyer's credit and line of credit cover protects a lending bank at 90 per cent against war, restrictions on transfer, protracted default and insolvency; overseas investment insurance covers equity and untied loans against war, expropriation and restrictions on remittances (no commercial risk cover, since the investor manages the venture), for 15 years extendable to a maximum of 20.

Procedures for banks and exporters, per the courseware: a bank with a financial guarantee files a notice of default within 4 months from the due date or one month from the date of recall, and claims within 6 months from lodging the notice; banks may extend finance without prior approval up to ECGC's Discretionary Limit but must notify; names on ECGC's Specific Approval List need prior approval; exporters submit shipment declarations by the 15th of each month, claims within 12 months of the due date of the unpaid bills (and within 360 days of the due date after the overdue declaration), must not compromise or give discounts without prior approval, must not ship further after a buyer's default without approval and need prior approval to extend bills; claims are paid to the bank that handled the documents; claims are not settled for more than four buyers in a policy period; settlement does not relieve the exporter of recovery, which is shared pro rata.

payload.title: Who bears which risk in an export deal
payload.core_explanation_md:
Trade across borders carries every domestic risk **and** more, because buyer and seller sit in different countries, goods and money travel in opposite directions, and the invoice may be in a third currency.

**By who carries it**
| Risk | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Buyer risk** | the seller may not be paid, or goods are rejected; the buyer's credit weakens |
| **Seller risk** | the buyer paid in advance and the seller **does not ship**, ships **poor quality**, or ships **late** |
| **Shipping risk** | trouble with carriers, handling agents, ports and transporters: goods **mishandled, abandoned, delivered wrongly**, strikes, **no containers**, piracy |
| **Other risks** | bank failure, settlement, competition, **fraudulent documents**, price, legal, spread, market risk |

**By nature**: **credit** (buyer cannot pay), **legal** (embargoes, remittance bans), **country and political** (laws, reserves, unrest), **operational** (strikes, system failures, errors) and **exchange** (currency moves against you, including a **stronger home currency** that makes you dearer than competitors).

payload.title: Cutting trade risk without adding new risk
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Tools**: act with care and **plan the movement of goods and money**; set **limits on counterparties**; buy **credit insurance** (it also covers country risk); use **forwards, futures and options** for exchange risk; time **inflows and outflows** of foreign exchange; hold **foreign currency accounts**.

**The warning**: the tool must be **understood and controllable**. A product the bank cannot control only **adds** risk to the original one.

payload.title: How a bank limits country risk: capital-linked limits and what counts
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Limits**: the **Board** sets country limits against the bank's **regulatory capital (Tier I + Tier II)**, with sub-limits if wished, and **reviews at least yearly**. No country limit may exceed **regulatory capital**, except the **insignificant-risk** category. RBI may set an **aggregate limit for the higher-risk categories**.

**What counts as exposure**
- **Funded**: cash and bank balances, deposit placements, investments, loans and advances, trade credits and receivables, vostro overdrafts.
- **Non-funded**: letters of credit, committed lines, guarantees, performance and bid bonds, **confirmation of foreign banks' LCs**.
- From **domestic and foreign branches** alike.

**Indirect country risk**: if **net funded exposure to a country is 1% or more of total assets**, indirect exposure (for instance a domestic borrower heavily dependent on that country) is also reckoned, at **50%**.

**Net basis**: gross exposure **minus collateral, guarantees and insurance**; netting is allowed for cash collateral, bank guarantees and credit insurance **from a lower-risk country** than the one the exposure is on.

payload.title: Grading countries: ECGC's seven categories
payload.core_explanation_md:
RBI expects banks to **grade countries** on factors such as political stability, international relations, economic policy, GDP, inflation, exchange rate volatility, level of foreign trade, balance of payments, external debt, reserves, IMF quotas, international rating and payment record. A bank with **no system of its own** may adopt **ECGC's classification**.

| Category | Risk |
| --- | --- |
| **A1** | insignificant |
| **A2** | low |
| **B1** | moderately low |
| **B2** | moderate |
| **C1** | moderately high |
| **C2** | high |
| **D** | very high |

**Open cover**: A1 to B2. **Restricted cover**: C1, C2 and D, where cover is by **specific approval** (valid six months in the courseware).

payload.title: ECGC: history, ownership and how it shares risk
payload.core_explanation_md:
**ECGC Ltd** is **wholly owned by the Government of India**, under the **Ministry of Commerce and Industry**, run by a Board with members from **Government, RBI, banking, insurance and exporters**.

**History**: **Export Risks Insurance Corporation (1957)**, which became the **Export Credit Guarantee Corporation (1964)**.

**Purpose**: promote exports, **protect exporters against failure of the buyer, bank or country**, supply **information on buyers, banks and countries**, and let **banks lend more** by insuring them.

**Risk sharing**: cover is **never 100%**; the exporter or bank bears part of the loss; **maximum cover is 90% to 95%**.

**Regulation**: ECGC schemes fall under **IRDAI**, so **premium on financial guarantees is paid up front** (one month's, from the previous year's average).

**Recoveries** are **shared in the same ratio** as the loss (for example **65:35**).

payload.title: The Shipment Comprehensive Risks policy: what it covers and what the exporter must do
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Policy**: **12 months**, **whole-turnover**, **declaration based**. All shipments are covered, but **letter of credit shipments may be excluded**. Exporters with expected turnover **above ₹5 crore** qualify.

**Risks covered, at 90%**: **commercial or buyer risk**, **political risk**, **LC opening bank risk**.

**What the exporter must do**
- Hold **credit limits** on buyers and opening banks.
- Keep **premium deposit** sufficient for the projected turnover.
- **Declare shipments monthly by the 15th** of the next month.
- **Declare bills unpaid more than 30 days** after due date by the 15th of the next month.
- **File the claim within 360 days of the due date** (or 540 days from policy expiry, if earlier).
- **Minimise loss**, pursue recovery, **share recoveries**.

**Perks**: **no claim bonus 5% up to 50%**.

**Not covered under standard policies**: commercial disputes, **causes inherent in the goods**, buyer's failure to obtain **import or exchange authorisation**, **default of an agent or collecting bank**, **exchange rate fluctuation**, and the **exporter's own failure or negligence**.

**Courseware difference**: the book describes **protracted default after about four months**; ECGC's current sheet asks for a declaration **after 30 days**.

payload.title: The other ECGC policies at a glance
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Policy | For |
| --- | --- |
| **Small Exporters Policy** | small exporters (a standard policy with extra concessions) |
| **Specific Shipment** | one-off **short-term (up to 180 days)**, deferred payment, buyer's credit, services, construction projects |
| **Exports (Specific Buyers)** | **all shipments to a named buyer** |
| **Buyer Exposure** | large exporters; cover on **expected exposure** to one buyer |
| **Export Turnover** | exporters paying **₹10 lakh or more** of premium a year |
| **Consignment Exports** | goods **stocked abroad** with an agent or global entity |
| **IT-Enabled Services (SITES)** | **one customer**, **80%** cover |
| **SME / Micro Exporters** | small manufacturing and service units, **90%** cover |
| **Customer specific** | large exporters, premium **over ₹10 lakh** |

payload.title: ECGC covers a bank can buy
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Cover | Protects the bank against |
| --- | --- |
| **Packing credit insurance** | loss on **pre-shipment** advances (manufacture, processing, purchase, packing against a firm order or LC), one-year cover |
| **ECIB WT-PC / WT-PS** | whole-turnover cover of **all packing credit** or **all post-shipment** advances; premium on **WT-PC borne by exporters**, on **WT-PS by the bank** |
| **Export Production Finance Guarantee** | pre-shipment advances against **incentives receivable** |
| **Export Finance Guarantee** | post-shipment advances against **cash assistance, duty drawback** |
| **Export Performance Indemnity** | losses on **guarantees the bank issues** for exporters (performance, bid bonds); a **counter-guarantee** |
| **Export Finance (Overseas Lending) Guarantee** | **foreign currency loan to an overseas project contractor** not repaid |
| **Transfer Guarantee** | the **foreign bank failing to reimburse** a **confirmed LC** |

payload.title: Special ECGC schemes: exchange cover, factoring, buyer's credit and investment insurance
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Exchange Fluctuation Risk Cover**: for payments due **beyond 12 months up to 15 years**. **Deductible 2% of the reference rate**: gains or losses **within 2%** stay with the exporter; **ECGC bears losses beyond 2% up to 35%** (and takes gains over 2% up to 35%).

**Maturity factoring**: **up to 90% finance**, credit protection against buyer default, a **sales ledger**, collection; for exporters on **open account** with a clean record.

**Buyer's credit / line of credit cover**: protects the **lending bank** at **90%** against **war, transfer restrictions, protracted default, insolvency**.

**Overseas investment insurance**: covers **equity and untied loans** against **war, expropriation and remittance restrictions**; **no commercial risk cover** because the investor shares in management; **15 years**, extendable to a **maximum of 20**.

payload.title: Notices, claims and recoveries: who must do what, and when
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Bank with a financial guarantee**
- **Notice of default** within **4 months of the due date** or **one month of recall**, whichever is earlier.
- **Claim within 6 months** of lodging the notice.
- Finance up to the **Discretionary Limit** needs only **notification**; names on the **Specific Approval List** need **prior approval**.

**Exporter**
- **Shipment declaration by the 15th** of each month.
- Claim within **12 months** of the due date of unpaid bills (and within **360 days** after the overdue declaration).
- **No compromise or discount** without prior approval; **no further shipment** to a defaulting buyer and **no extension of bills** without approval.

**Claims**: paid to the **bank that handled the documents**; **not more than four buyers** per policy period; settlement **does not release the exporter** from recovery, which is **shared pro rata**.

payload.title: Sharing a recovery with ECGC
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: a bank advanced ₹80,00,000 against an export bill. The insurance cover is 65% and ECGC settles the claim on the outstanding advance. The bank later recovers ₹30,00,000 from collateral. How much does the bank pass on to ECGC and how much does it keep?

worked_steps.description: ECGC pays the cover share of the outstanding advance.
The recovery is shared in the same ratio, 65:35.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: The bank pays ₹19,50,000 of the recovery to ECGC and keeps ₹10,50,000

self_check.prompt_text: Why must the bank hand over part of the recovery even though ECGC has already paid its claim?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Cover is on a risk-sharing basis, so recoveries are shared in the same ratio as the loss; settlement of a claim does not give the bank the whole recovery.

payload.title: What the exchange fluctuation cover pays
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: an exporter expects USD 500,000 under a contract with payments beyond 12 months, covered by the Exchange Fluctuation Risk Cover scheme at a reference rate of ₹84.00. At settlement the rate is ₹80.00. How much does ECGC pay, taking the 2% deductible and the 35% ceiling as in the courseware?

worked_steps.description: Loss per USD against the reference rate.
As a percentage of the reference rate.
The exporter bears the first 2% of the reference rate.
ECGC bears the balance, which is below the 35% ceiling.

self_check.prompt_text: If the rate had fallen only to ₹83.00, what would ECGC pay?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The loss of ₹1.00 is 1.19% of the reference rate, within the 2% deductible, so ECGC pays nothing.

payload.stem_md: A buyer abroad takes delivery of goods but never pays. Which risk is this, by who bears it?

options.explanation_md: Seller risk is the buyer's exposure to the seller's failure to ship.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Non-payment by the buyer is buyer risk, which the seller faces.

options.explanation_md: No change in law is involved.
A currency move that changes the rupee value.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Adverse movement in currencies, including a stronger home currency, is exchange risk.

options.text_md: Using forward covers for exchange risk

payload.stem_md: What is the highest limit a bank may set for exposure to a country that is not in the insignificant risk category?

The bank must close the exposure

options.text_md: A loan to a foreign company
Confirmation of a foreign bank's letter of credit

payload.stem_md: In ECGC's seven-fold classification, which category denotes very high risk?
payload.correct_explanation_md: A1 is insignificant, A2 low, B1 moderately low, B2 moderate, C1 moderately high, C2 high, D very high.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Banks without their own system may adopt the ECGC country risk classification.

payload.stem_md: A bank advanced ₹60,00,000 against an export bill covered at 70%. ECGC pays the claim on the outstanding advance, and the bank later recovers ₹25,00,000. How much of the recovery must the bank pay to ECGC, in rupees?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Recoveries are shared in the same ratio as the cover. 70% of ₹25,00,000 = ₹17,50,000.

payload.stem_md: A bank has net funded exposure to a country of ₹4,200 crore and indirect exposures of ₹1,600 crore. Its total assets are ₹2,50,000 crore. Total exposure counted for that country, with indirect exposure taken in as the Directions require, is how many crore rupees?
payload.correct_explanation_md: One per cent of total assets = ₹2,500 crore. Net funded exposure of ₹4,200 crore exceeds it, so indirect exposure is reckoned at 50%: 1,600 × 50% = 800. Total = 4,200 + 800 = ₹5,000 crore.

worked_solution_steps.description: One per cent of total assets

unresolved: ECGC product detail (small exporters limit, protracted default period, bank cover percentages and premiums, claim periods) comes from the courseware, whose edition predates ECGC's current literature. Only the Shipment Comprehensive Risks sheet (undated) was read from ECGC; the ECIB sales literature PDF could not be read as text. Where the two differ the item notes it. Percentages and premium rates for the bank covers are not taught.

The Reserve Bank directions on country risk provisioning (graded provisions from 0.25 to 100 per cent) are in the Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning Directions, 2025, which were seen only through a secondary reproduction; provisioning percentages are not taught. The courseware's statement that a provision is required at 1 per cent of total assets is not used as an exam fact.
The RBI Concentration Risk Management Directions copy used is updated to 1 October 2026, after the cut-off; Chapter VII was used and amendments since 28 November 2025 were not compared.
The courseware cites the country classification at 31 December 2021; the figures are dated and are not taught. ECGC's list effective 1 January 2026 was saved but not used.

items.title: Who bears which risk in an export deal
items.core_explanation_md:
Trade across borders carries every domestic risk **and** more, because buyer and seller sit in different countries, goods and money travel in opposite directions, and the invoice may be in a third currency.

**By who carries it**
| Risk | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Buyer risk** | the seller may not be paid, or goods are rejected; the buyer's credit weakens |
| **Seller risk** | the buyer paid in advance and the seller **does not ship**, ships **poor quality**, or ships **late** |
| **Shipping risk** | trouble with carriers, handling agents, ports and transporters: goods **mishandled, abandoned, delivered wrongly**, strikes, **no containers**, piracy |
| **Other risks** | bank failure, settlement, competition, **fraudulent documents**, price, legal, spread, market risk |

**By nature**: **credit** (buyer cannot pay), **legal** (embargoes, remittance bans), **country and political** (laws, reserves, unrest), **operational** (strikes, system failures, errors) and **exchange** (currency moves against you, including a **stronger home currency** that makes you dearer than competitors).

items.title: Cutting trade risk without adding new risk
items.core_explanation_md:
**Tools**: act with care and **plan the movement of goods and money**; set **limits on counterparties**; buy **credit insurance** (it also covers country risk); use **forwards, futures and options** for exchange risk; time **inflows and outflows** of foreign exchange; hold **foreign currency accounts**.

**The warning**: the tool must be **understood and controllable**. A product the bank cannot control only **adds** risk to the original one.

items.title: How a bank limits country risk: capital-linked limits and what counts
items.core_explanation_md:
**Limits**: the **Board** sets country limits against the bank's **regulatory capital (Tier I + Tier II)**, with sub-limits if wished, and **reviews at least yearly**. No country limit may exceed **regulatory capital**, except the **insignificant-risk** category. RBI may set an **aggregate limit for the higher-risk categories**.

**What counts as exposure**
- **Funded**: cash and bank balances, deposit placements, investments, loans and advances, trade credits and receivables, vostro overdrafts.
- **Non-funded**: letters of credit, committed lines, guarantees, performance and bid bonds, **confirmation of foreign banks' LCs**.
- From **domestic and foreign branches** alike.

**Indirect country risk**: if **net funded exposure to a country is 1% or more of total assets**, indirect exposure (for instance a domestic borrower heavily dependent on that country) is also reckoned, at **50%**.

**Net basis**: gross exposure **minus collateral, guarantees and insurance**; netting is allowed for cash collateral, bank guarantees and credit insurance **from a lower-risk country** than the one the exposure is on.

items.title: Grading countries: ECGC's seven categories
items.core_explanation_md:
RBI expects banks to **grade countries** on factors such as political stability, international relations, economic policy, GDP, inflation, exchange rate volatility, level of foreign trade, balance of payments, external debt, reserves, IMF quotas, international rating and payment record. A bank with **no system of its own** may adopt **ECGC's classification**.

| Category | Risk |
| --- | --- |
| **A1** | insignificant |
| **A2** | low |
| **B1** | moderately low |
| **B2** | moderate |
| **C1** | moderately high |
| **C2** | high |
| **D** | very high |

**Open cover**: A1 to B2. **Restricted cover**: C1, C2 and D, where cover is by **specific approval** (valid six months in the courseware).

items.title: ECGC: history, ownership and how it shares risk
items.core_explanation_md:
**ECGC Ltd** is **wholly owned by the Government of India**, under the **Ministry of Commerce and Industry**, run by a Board with members from **Government, RBI, banking, insurance and exporters**.

**History**: **Export Risks Insurance Corporation (1957)**, which became the **Export Credit Guarantee Corporation (1964)**.

**Purpose**: promote exports, **protect exporters against failure of the buyer, bank or country**, supply **information on buyers, banks and countries**, and let **banks lend more** by insuring them.

**Risk sharing**: cover is **never 100%**; the exporter or bank bears part of the loss; **maximum cover is 90% to 95%**.

**Regulation**: ECGC schemes fall under **IRDAI**, so **premium on financial guarantees is paid up front** (one month's, from the previous year's average).

**Recoveries** are **shared in the same ratio** as the loss (for example **65:35**).

items.title: The Shipment Comprehensive Risks policy: what it covers and what the exporter must do
items.core_explanation_md:
**Policy**: **12 months**, **whole-turnover**, **declaration based**. All shipments are covered, but **letter of credit shipments may be excluded**. Exporters with expected turnover **above ₹5 crore** qualify.

**Risks covered, at 90%**: **commercial or buyer risk**, **political risk**, **LC opening bank risk**.

**What the exporter must do**
- Hold **credit limits** on buyers and opening banks.
- Keep **premium deposit** sufficient for the projected turnover.
- **Declare shipments monthly by the 15th** of the next month.
- **Declare bills unpaid more than 30 days** after due date by the 15th of the next month.
- **File the claim within 360 days of the due date** (or 540 days from policy expiry, if earlier).
- **Minimise loss**, pursue recovery, **share recoveries**.

**Perks**: **no claim bonus 5% up to 50%**.

**Not covered under standard policies**: commercial disputes, **causes inherent in the goods**, buyer's failure to obtain **import or exchange authorisation**, **default of an agent or collecting bank**, **exchange rate fluctuation**, and the **exporter's own failure or negligence**.

**Courseware difference**: the book describes **protracted default after about four months**; ECGC's current sheet asks for a declaration **after 30 days**.

items.title: ECGC covers a bank can buy
items.core_explanation_md:
| Cover | Protects the bank against |
| --- | --- |
| **Packing credit insurance** | loss on **pre-shipment** advances (manufacture, processing, purchase, packing against a firm order or LC), one-year cover |
| **ECIB WT-PC / WT-PS** | whole-turnover cover of **all packing credit** or **all post-shipment** advances; premium on **WT-PC borne by exporters**, on **WT-PS by the bank** |
| **Export Production Finance Guarantee** | pre-shipment advances against **incentives receivable** |
| **Export Finance Guarantee** | post-shipment advances against **cash assistance, duty drawback** |
| **Export Performance Indemnity** | losses on **guarantees the bank issues** for exporters (performance, bid bonds); a **counter-guarantee** |
| **Export Finance (Overseas Lending) Guarantee** | **foreign currency loan to an overseas project contractor** not repaid |
| **Transfer Guarantee** | the **foreign bank failing to reimburse** a **confirmed LC** |

items.title: Special ECGC schemes: exchange cover, factoring, buyer's credit and investment insurance
items.core_explanation_md:
**Exchange Fluctuation Risk Cover**: for payments due **beyond 12 months up to 15 years**. **Deductible 2% of the reference rate**: gains or losses **within 2%** stay with the exporter; **ECGC bears losses beyond 2% up to 35%** (and takes gains over 2% up to 35%).

**Maturity factoring**: **up to 90% finance**, credit protection against buyer default, a **sales ledger**, collection; for exporters on **open account** with a clean record.

**Buyer's credit / line of credit cover**: protects the **lending bank** at **90%** against **war, transfer restrictions, protracted default, insolvency**.

**Overseas investment insurance**: covers **equity and untied loans** against **war, expropriation and remittance restrictions**; **no commercial risk cover** because the investor shares in management; **15 years**, extendable to a **maximum of 20**.

items.title: Notices, claims and recoveries: who must do what, and when
items.core_explanation_md:
**Bank with a financial guarantee**
- **Notice of default** within **4 months of the due date** or **one month of recall**, whichever is earlier.
- **Claim within 6 months** of lodging the notice.
- Finance up to the **Discretionary Limit** needs only **notification**; names on the **Specific Approval List** need **prior approval**.

**Exporter**
- **Shipment declaration by the 15th** of each month.
- Claim within **12 months** of the due date of unpaid bills (and within **360 days** after the overdue declaration).
- **No compromise or discount** without prior approval; **no further shipment** to a defaulting buyer and **no extension of bills** without approval.

**Claims**: paid to the **bank that handled the documents**; **not more than four buyers** per policy period; settlement **does not release the exporter** from recovery, which is **shared pro rata**.

items.title: Sharing a recovery with ECGC
items.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: a bank advanced ₹80,00,000 against an export bill. The insurance cover is 65% and ECGC settles the claim on the outstanding advance. The bank later recovers ₹30,00,000 from collateral. How much does the bank pass on to ECGC and how much does it keep?

worked_steps.description: ECGC pays the cover share of the outstanding advance.
The recovery is shared in the same ratio, 65:35.

items.final_answer_with_unit: The bank pays ₹19,50,000 of the recovery to ECGC and keeps ₹10,50,000

self_check.prompt_text: Why must the bank hand over part of the recovery even though ECGC has already paid its claim?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Cover is on a risk-sharing basis, so recoveries are shared in the same ratio as the loss; settlement of a claim does not give the bank the whole recovery.
